claim: Pairwise models are commonly used to describe many-species communities.
source: Pairwise models are commonly used to describe many-species communities.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of pairwise models in the field, representing established practice.

claim: In pairwise models, an individual receives additive fitness effects from pairwise interactions with each species in the community.
source: In these models, an individual receives additive fitness effects from pairwise interactions with each species in the community ('additivity assumption').
evidence: This defines a fundamental assumption of pairwise models as described in the manuscript.

claim: All pairwise interactions are typically represented by a single equation where parameters reflect signs and strengths of fitness effects.
source: All pairwise interactions are typically represented by a single equation where parameters reflect signs and strengths of fitness effects ('universality assumption').
evidence: This describes the universality assumption of pairwise models as a standard practice in the field.

claim: A single equation fails to qualitatively capture diverse pairwise microbial interactions.
source: Here, we show that a single equation fails to qualitatively capture diverse pairwise microbial interactions.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the mechanistic models and analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Different equations are appropriate depending on whether a mediator is consumable or reusable.
source: Different equations are appropriate depending on whether a mediator is consumable or reusable, whether an interaction is mediated by one or more mediators, and sometimes even on quantitative details of the community (e.g. relative fitness of the two species, initial conditions).
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through analytical derivations and numerical simulations in the Results section.

claim: Different equations are appropriate depending on whether an interaction is mediated by one or more mediators.
source: Different equations are appropriate depending on whether a mediator is consumable or reusable, whether an interaction is mediated by one or more mediators, and sometimes even on quantitative details of the community (e.g. relative fitness of the two species, initial conditions).
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis of two-mediator interactions in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: Different equations are sometimes appropriate depending on quantitative details of the community such as relative fitness of the two species and initial conditions.
source: Different equations are appropriate depending on whether a mediator is consumable or reusable, whether an interaction is mediated by one or more mediators, and sometimes even on quantitative details of the community (e.g. relative fitness of the two species, initial conditions).
evidence: This is demonstrated through various cases in Figure 3 and Figure 4 showing how initial conditions and relative fitness affect model choice.

claim: Pairwise modeling will often fail to predict microbial dynamics due to potential violation of the additivity assumption in many-species communities.
source: Our results, combined with potential violation of the additivity assumption in many-species communities, suggest that pairwise modeling will often fail to predict microbial dynamics.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the results presented in the manuscript combined with known issues with the additivity assumption.

claim: Microbial communities are important for industrial applications such as cheese and wine fermentation.
source: Microbial communities are important for industrial applications such as cheese and wine fermentation (van Hijum et al., 2013) and municipal waste treatment (Seghezzo et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial communities are important for municipal waste treatment.
source: Microbial communities are important for industrial applications such as cheese and wine fermentation (van Hijum et al., 2013) and municipal waste treatment (Seghezzo et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbial communities can modulate immune responses and food digestion during health and disease.
source: Microbial communities are also important for human health: they can modulate immune responses and food digestion (Round and Mazmanian, 2009; Kau et al., 2011) during health and disease.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Properties of the entire community are influenced by interactions wherein individuals alter the physiology of other individuals.
source: Properties of the entire community ('community properties', e.g. species dynamics, ability to survive internal or external perturbations, and biochemical activities of the entire community) are influenced by interactions wherein individuals alter the physiology of other individuals (Widder et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Choosing the appropriate mathematical model to describe species interactions is critical to understand and predict community properties.
source: To understand and predict community properties, choosing the appropriate mathematical model to describe species interactions is critical.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the importance of model selection in ecology.

claim: It is often unclear a priori what the minimal essential details are for a mathematical model.
source: A mathematical model ideally focuses only on details that are essential to community properties of interest. However, it is often unclear a priori what the minimal essential details are.
evidence: This reflects a general challenge in mathematical modeling acknowledged in the field.

claim: Mechanistic models explicitly consider interaction mediators as state variables.
source: We define 'mechanistic models' as models that explicitly consider interaction mediators as state variables.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the purposes of this manuscript.

claim: Lotka-Volterra pairwise models only consider the fitness effects of interactions.
source: In contrast, Lotka-Volterra ('L-V') pairwise models only consider the fitness effects of interactions.
evidence: This describes a fundamental characteristic of L-V pairwise models as commonly understood in the field.

claim: L-V models assume that the fitness of an individual is the sum of its basal fitness and fitness influences from pairwise interactions with individuals of the same species and of every other species in the community.
source: Specifically, L-V models assume that the fitness of an individual is the sum of its basal fitness (the net growth rate of an individual in isolation) and fitness influences from pairwise interactions with individuals of the same species and of every other species in the community ('additivity' assumption).
evidence: This describes the additivity assumption that is fundamental to L-V pairwise models.

claim: L-V pairwise modeling has successfully explained the oscillatory dynamics of hare and its predator lynx.
source: L-V pairwise modeling has successfully explained the oscillatory dynamics of hare and its predator lynx (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Volterra, 1926; Wangersky, 1978; BiologyEOC, 2016).
evidence: This is a well-known historical success of L-V models, supported by citations and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Pairwise models have been instrumental in delineating conditions for multiple carnivores to coexist when competing for herbivores.
source: Pairwise models have also been instrumental in delineating conditions for multiple carnivores to coexist when competing for herbivores (MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the hare-lynx example, both species are also interaction mediators, and therefore pairwise and mechanistic models are identical.
source: In the hare-lynx example, both species are also interaction mediators, and therefore pairwise and mechanistic models are identical.
evidence: This is an explanation provided by the authors for why pairwise models work in this case.

claim: If herbivores rapidly reach steady state, herbivores can be mathematically eliminated from the mechanistic model to yield a pairwise model of competing carnivores.
source: In the second example, if herbivores (mediators of competitive interactions between carnivores) rapidly reach steady state, herbivores can be mathematically eliminated from the mechanistic model to yield a pairwise model of competing carnivores (MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pairwise models are often used to predict how perturbations to steady-state species composition exacerbate or decline over time.
source: Pairwise models are often used to predict how perturbations to steady-state species composition exacerbate or decline over time (May, 1972; Thébault and Fontaine, 2010; Mougi and Kondoh, 2012; Allesina and Tang, 2012; Suweis et al., 2013; Coyte et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Many interactions in microbial communities are mediated by chemicals.
source: The temptation of using pairwise models is indeed high, including in microbial communities where many interactions are mediated by chemicals (Mounier et al., 2008; Faust and Raes, 2012; Stein et al., 2013; Marino et al., 2014; Coyte et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanistic models would require knowledge of chemical mediators, which are often challenging to identify.
source: Mechanistic models would require knowledge of chemical mediators, which are often challenging to identify.
evidence: This reflects a practical challenge in constructing mechanistic models for microbial communities.

claim: Mechanistic models require more equations and parameters than their cognate pairwise models.
source: Since chemical mediators are explicitly modeled, mechanistic models require more equations and parameters than their cognate pairwise models (Figure 1, Table).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the mechanistic and pairwise models shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pairwise model parameters are relatively easy to estimate using community dynamics or dynamics of monocultures and pairwise cocultures.
source: Pairwise model parameters are relatively easy to estimate using community dynamics or dynamics of monocultures and pairwise cocultures (Mounier et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2013; Guo and Boedicker, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pairwise modeling has been liberally applied to microbial communities.
source: Consequently, pairwise modeling has been liberally applied to microbial communities.
evidence: This is an observation about the prevalence of pairwise modeling in microbiology.

claim: A third species can influence interactions between a species pair, which sometimes violates the additivity assumption of pairwise models.
source: This is because a third species can influence interactions between a species pair ('indirect interactions'), which sometimes violates the additivity assumption of pairwise models.
evidence: This is a known issue with pairwise models in multispecies communities, supported by the citations in the previous claim.

claim: A carnivore can indirectly increase the density of a plant by decreasing the density of an herbivore.
source: For example, a carnivore can indirectly increase the density of a plant by decreasing the density of an herbivore ('interaction chain'; 'density-mediated indirect interactions').
evidence: This is a classic example of an interaction chain in ecology.

claim: A carnivore can decrease how often an herbivore forages plants.
source: A carnivore can also decrease how often an herbivore forages plants ('interaction modification', 'trait-mediated indirect interactions', or 'higher order interactions') (Vandermeer, 1969; Wootton, 1994; Billick and Case, 1994; Wootton, 2002).
evidence: This is an example of interaction modification, supported by citations.

claim: Interaction modification violates the additivity assumption.
source: Interaction modification (but not interaction chain) violates the additivity assumption (Methods-Interaction modification but not interaction chain violates the additivity assumption) (Tilman, 1987; Wootton, 1994; Schmitz et al., 2004) and can cause the pairwise model to generate qualitatively wrong predictions.
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically in the Methods section and supported by citations.

claim: Interaction chain does not violate the additivity assumption.
source: Interaction modification (but not interaction chain) violates the additivity assumption (Methods-Interaction modification but not interaction chain violates the additivity assumption) (Tilman, 1987; Wootton, 1994; Schmitz et al., 2004) and can cause the pairwise model to generate qualitatively wrong predictions.
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically in the Methods section and supported by citations.

claim: Pairwise models largely failed to predict biomass and species coexistence in three-species and seven-species plant communities.
source: Indeed, pairwise models largely failed to predict biomass and species coexistence in three-species and seven-species plant communities (Dormann and Roxburgh, 2005), although reported failures of pairwise models could be due to limitations in data collection and analysis (Case and Bender, 1981; Billick and Case, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microbes often influence other microbes via consumable metabolites, reusable signaling molecules, or a combination of chemicals.
source: Microbes often influence other microbes in a myriad of fashions, via consumable metabolites, reusable signaling molecules, or a combination of chemicals (Figure 2).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2 and represents common knowledge about microbial interactions.

claim: An L-V pairwise model and a mechanistic model both correctly predicted ratio stabilization and spatial intermixing between two strongly-cooperating populations exchanging diffusible essential metabolites.
source: For example, an L-V pairwise model and a mechanistic model both correctly predicted ratio stabilization and spatial intermixing between two strongly-cooperating populations exchanging diffusible essential metabolites (Momeni et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pairwise models largely captured competition outcomes and metabolic activities of three-species and four-species artificial microbial communities.
source: In other examples, pairwise models largely captured competition outcomes and metabolic activities of three-species and four-species artificial microbial communities (Vandermeer, 1969; Guo and Boedicker, 2016; Friedman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pairwise models often failed to predict species coexistence in seven-species microbial communities.
source: On the other hand, pairwise models often failed to predict species coexistence in seven-species microbial communities (Friedman et al., 2017), although this could be due to interaction modification discussed above.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A mechanistic reference model offers the advantage that community dynamics is deterministically known.
source: A mechanistic reference model offers several advantages: community dynamics is deterministically known; deriving a pairwise model is not limited by inaccuracy of experimental methods; and the flexibility in creating different reference models allows us to explore a variety of interaction mechanisms.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the advantages of using mechanistic models as references.

claim: Deriving a pairwise model from a mechanistic reference model is not limited by inaccuracy of experimental methods.
source: A mechanistic reference model offers several advantages: community dynamics is deterministically known; deriving a pairwise model is not limited by inaccuracy of experimental methods; and the flexibility in creating different reference models allows us to explore a variety of interaction mechanisms.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the advantages of using mechanistic models as references.

claim: The flexibility in creating different reference models allows exploration of a variety of interaction mechanisms.
source: A mechanistic reference model offers several advantages: community dynamics is deterministically known; deriving a pairwise model is not limited by inaccuracy of experimental methods; and the flexibility in creating different reference models allows us to explore a variety of interaction mechanisms.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the advantages of using mechanistic models as references.

claim: A well-mixed environment can be found in industrial fermenters.
source: A well-mixed environment can be found in industrial fermenters.
evidence: This is a statement about where well-mixed environments occur in practice.

claim: At a sufficiently small spatial scale, a spatially-structured environment can be approximated as a well-mixed environment.
source: Moreover, at a sufficiently small spatial scale, a spatially-structured environment can be approximated as a well-mixed environment, as chemicals are uniformly-distributed locally.
evidence: This is a logical statement about spatial scales and approximations.

claim: Motile organisms reduce the degree of spatial structure.
source: Motile organisms also reduce the degree of spatial structure.
evidence: This is a general principle about how organism motility affects spatial structure.

claim: A well-mixed environment allows the use of ordinary differential equations, which are more tractable than partial differential equations demanded by a spatially-structured environment.
source: A well-mixed environment allows us to use ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which are more tractable than partial differential equations demanded by a spatially-structured environment.
evidence: This is a statement about the mathematical advantages of assuming a well-mixed environment.

claim: For a reusable mediator, the mechanistic model can be transformed into a saturable L-V pairwise model after the concentration of the mediator has acclimated to be proportional to the producer population size.
source: When C1 is reusable, the mechanistic model (Figure 3A,i) can be transformed into a saturable L-V pairwise model (compare Figure 3A,ii with Equation 3), especially after the concentration of the mediator (which is initially zero) has acclimated to be proportional to the producer population size (Figure 3A legend; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For a reusable mediator, the saturable L-V pairwise model is valid regardless of whether the producer coexists with the consumer, outcompetes the consumer, or is outcompeted by the consumer.
source: This saturable L-V pairwise model is valid regardless of whether the producer coexists with the consumer, outcompetes the consumer, or is outcompeted by the consumer.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analytical derivation for reusable mediators.

claim: When supplier S1 always grows faster than consumer S2, C1 will eventually accumulate proportionally to S1.
source: Case I: When supplier S1 always grows faster than consumer S2 (the basal fitness of S1 is higher than the maximal fitness of S2), C1 will eventually accumulate proportionally to S1 (Figure 4A left; Methods-Deriving a pairwise model for interactions mediated by a single consumable mediator Case I).
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically in the Methods section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When C1 accumulates proportionally to S1, C1 may be approximated as a reusable mediator and can be predicted by the saturable L-V pairwise model.
source: In this case, C1 may be approximated as a reusable mediator and can be predicted by the saturable L-V pairwise model (Figure 4A right, compare dotted and solid lines).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A where the saturable L-V model matches the mechanistic model.

claim: The saturable L-V model and the alternative model are not interchangeable.
source: The saturable L-V model and the alternative model are not interchangeable (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 where the two models produce different predictions.

claim: When one species affects another species via multiple mediators, in general, these mediators may not be regarded as a single mediator nor representable by a single pairwise model.
source: If one species influences another species through multiple mediators, then in general, these mediators may not be regarded as a single mediator nor representable by a single pairwise model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of two-mediator interactions in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: For two reusable mediators, unless their potencies are similar or one mediator is much more potent than the other, saturable L-V model parameters can qualitatively differ depending on initial community density.
source: For example, for two reusable mediators, unless their potencies are similar or one mediator is much more potent than the other, saturable L-V model parameters can qualitatively differ depending on initial community density (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A pairwise model derived from a high-density community generates false predictions for low-density communities when mediators have different potencies.
source: Consequently, a pairwise model derived from a high-density community generates false predictions for low-density communities (Figure 5C), limiting the usefulness of pairwise models.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5C.

claim: For a competitive commensal community, the best-fitting L-V pairwise model can predict future dynamics in some but not all communities, depending on parameters used in the mechanistic model.
source: We find that the best-fitting L-V pairwise model can predict future dynamics in some but not all communities, depending on parameters used in the mechanistic model (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 where the pairwise model works in some cases but not others.

claim: When indirect interactions take the form of interaction chains, if each chain segment of two species engages in an independent interaction and can be represented by a pairwise model, then multispecies pairwise models can work.
source: When indirect interactions take the form of interaction chains, if each chain segment of two species engages in an independent interaction and can be represented by a pairwise model, then multispecies pairwise models can work (Figure 7A-B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A-B.

claim: When indirect interactions take the form of interaction modification, even if each species pair can be accurately represented by a pairwise model, a multispecies pairwise model may fail.
source: When indirect interactions take the form of interaction modification, even if each species pair can be accurately represented by a pairwise model, a multispecies pairwise model may fail (Figure 7C–F, ).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Mediator modification is very common in microbial communities.
source: Mediator modification is very common in microbial communities.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about microbial communities.

claim: Antibiotic released by one species to inhibit another species may be inactivated by a third species, and this type of indirect interactions can stabilize microbial communities.
source: For example, antibiotic released by one species to inhibit another species may be inactivated by a third species, and this type of indirect interactions can stabilize microbial communities (Kelsic et al., 2015; Bairey et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In oral biofilms, organic acids such as lactic acid are generated from carbohydrate fermentation by many species.
source: For example in oral biofilms, organic acids such as lactic acid are generated from carbohydrate fermentation by many species (Bradshaw et al., 1994; Marsh and Bradshaw, 1997; Kuramitsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Organic acid by-products are consumed by multiple species in oral biofilms.
source: Such by-products are also consumed by multiple species (Kolenbrander, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pairwise models have been instrumental in understanding ecological phenomena such as prey-predator oscillatory dynamics and coexistence of competing predator species.
source: First, pairwise models have been instrumental in understanding ecological phenomena such as prey-predator oscillatory dynamics and coexistence of competing predator species (Volterra, 1926; MacArthur, 1970; Case and Casten, 1979; Chesson, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Vetsigian et al. found that interactions between soil-isolated Streptomyces strains are enriched for reciprocity.
source: For example, Vetsigian et al., 2011 found that interactions between soil-isolated Streptomyces strains are enriched for reciprocity – if A inhibits or promotes B, it is likely that B also inhibits or promotes A (Vetsigian et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pairwise models have been useful in qualitatively understanding species assembly rules in small communities.
source: Third, pairwise models have been useful in qualitatively understanding species assembly rules in small communities (Friedman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Qualitative information regarding species survival in competitions among a small number of species may be used to predict survival in more diverse communities within a similar time window.
source: That is, qualitative information regarding species survival in competitions among a small number of species may be used to predict survival in more diverse communities within a similar time window.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the work cited in the previous claim.

claim: A pairwise model can serve as a starting point for generating hypotheses on species interactions.
source: Fourth, a pairwise model can serve as a starting point for generating hypotheses on species interactions (e.g. Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Stein et al. used 2/3 of community dynamics data as a training set to derive a multispecies pairwise model, and in the best-case scenario, the model generated reasonable predictions on the remaining 1/3 of data.
source: For example, Stein et al. used 2/3 of community dynamics data as a training set to derive a multispecies pairwise model, and in the best-case scenario, the model generated reasonable predictions on the remaining 1/3 of data (Stein et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Predicting qualitative consequences of species removal or addition using a pairwise model has encountered difficulties, especially in communities of more than three species.
source: Not surprisingly, predicting qualitative consequences of species removal or addition using a pairwise model has encountered difficulties, especially in communities of more than three species (Mounier et al., 2008; Friedman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tilman argued that if a small number of mechanisms could explain much of the observed pattern, then this abstraction would be highly revealing.
source: For example, Tilman argued that if a small number of mechanisms (e.g. the 'axes of trade-offs' in species traits) could explain much of the observed pattern (e.g. species coexistence), then this abstraction would be highly revealing (Tilman, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The choice of abstraction is often not obvious.
source: However, the choice of abstraction is often not obvious.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenge of choosing the right level of abstraction in modeling.

claim: Knowledge of mechanisms may eventually help determine the right level of abstraction.
source: This simple example, inspired by extracellular breakdown of cellulose into a consumable sugar C (Bayer and Lamed, 1986; Felix and Ljungdahl, 1993; Schwarz, 2001), illustrates how knowledge of mechanisms may eventually help us determine the right level of abstraction.
evidence: This is illustrated through the example in Figure 8 and supported by citations.

claim: If we do not know whether a pairwise model is valid, we need to be cautious since pairwise models can fail to even qualitatively capture pairwise microbial interactions.
source: However, if we do not know whether a pairwise model is valid, we will need to be cautious since pairwise models can fail to even qualitatively capture pairwise microbial interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: We need to be careful when extrapolating and generalizing conclusions obtained from pairwise models, especially for communities where species interaction mechanisms are diverse.
source: We need to be equally careful when extrapolating and generalizing conclusions obtained from pairwise models, especially for communities where species interaction mechanisms are diverse.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The authors advocate a transition to models that incorporate interaction mechanisms at the appropriate level of abstraction.
source: Considering recent advances in identifying and quantifying interactions, we advocate a transition to models that incorporate interaction mechanisms at the appropriate level of abstraction.
evidence: This is a recommendation made by the authors based on their findings.
